questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD basics: ConfigMap-driven content, Pod specs with probes, RBAC-lite concepts via namespace policies, and basic networking isolation.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap as volume source for static content
- Pod readiness/liveness probes
- Resource requests/limits
- ConfigMap-driven rolling updates via annotation
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: site-content
data:
  index.html: |-
    <html><body>Hello</body></html>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-site
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: static-site
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        site-content-hash: "<hash>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: site-content
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: site-content
        configMap:
          name: site-content
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate updating the site content without full redeploys?
- What are the trade-offs of using a ConfigMap for large HTML content?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to reason about per-namespace security controls, init workflows, and practical use of ConfigMaps/Secrets with network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for prep tasks and tooling installation
- Image scanning with Trivy in-cluster
- Per-namespace heartbeat and audit via ConfigMap
- Secrets for registry credentials and policy ConfigMaps
- NetworkPolicy restricting egress to vulnerability DB

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the image-scan guard
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-scan-guard
  namespace: TARGET_NS
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: image-scan-guard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-scan-guard
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl ca-certificates && mkdir -p /logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: guard
        image: busybox:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: registry-creds
        - configMapRef:
            name: scan-policy
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: image-scan-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale this to large clusters with many namespaces? 
- How would you handle false positives and performance impact during pod startup?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD ability to compose a small, namespace-scoped verification workflow that touches ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, and network policy.

## Key Concepts
- Deployment with InitContainer
- ConfigMap-based allowlist
- Secret-based credentials and TLS sidecar
- PVC-mounted /secrets and lightweight parsing with jq/yq
- Readiness/Liveness probes and per-namespace NetworkPolicy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: compliance-api-creds
  namespace: default
data:
  token: <base64>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: secret-allowlist
  namespace: default
data:
  allowed_keys: |
    tls.key
    tls.crt
    creds
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secret-compliance-checker
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: secret-compliance-checker
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache jq curl && wget -O - https://github.com/yq-dev/yq/releases/latest/download/yq_linux_amd64 -O /usr/local/bin/yq && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/yq"]
      containers:
        - name: checker
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "./check.sh"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: secrets
              mountPath: /secrets
      volumes:
        - name: secrets
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: secret-storage
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale and test this in a real cluster?
- What are risks with mounting Secrets in /secrets and how to mitigate?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to architect cross-resource automation in a namespace, combining CronJob, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and deployment rollouts with proper observability and network controls.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scheduling and idempotent config sync
- ConfigMaps vs Secrets for config data
- Rolling restarts via deployment annotations
- InitContainers for tooling setup
- Logs stored on a PVC
- NetworkPolicy scoping egress to a single service

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: config-sync
spec:
  schedule: "*/2 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl"]
          containers:
            - name: config-fetch
              image: curlimages/curl:8.0.1
              envFrom:
                - secretRef:
                    name: config-token
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer ${API_TOKEN}' https://config-service.local/api/v1/env?ns=${NAMESPACE} | script/process-config.sh && kubectl -n ${NAMESPACE} annotate deploy --overwrite canary-updateTime=$(date +%s)" ]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: app-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure the ConfigMap update is atomic and avoid partial writes?
- How would you scale this to many namespaces without duplicating secrets or causing race conditions?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to translate dynamic allowlists into enforced Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules while maintaining per-namespace isolation. It combines ConfigMap-driven configuration, DNS resolution, RBAC scoping, and observability—all core CKAD competencies.

## Key Concepts

- **NetworkPolicy**: Enforces egress rules at the pod level using `ipBlock` selectors. Note that egress rules require CNI support for enforcement.
- **ConfigMap**: Serves as the externalized allowlist store, allowing updates without pod or job restarts.
- **CronJob**: Periodically reconciles the allowlist state with the active NetworkPolicy, acting as a controller loop.
- **InitContainer**: Ensures required tools are available before the main container starts, though using a pre-built image with curl is simpler.
- **PVC**: Provides persistent storage for test results, enabling post-job analysis and debugging.

## Common Pitfalls

- Forgetting DNS egress rules causes complete name resolution failure
- Using `0.0.0.0/0` with broad `except` blocks can create confusing policies
- Resolving hostnames to IPs at apply time introduces a lag between DNS changes and policy updates
- Not all CNIs fully support egress policies; test enforcement in your target environment

## Production Considerations

- Add error handling and alerting for resolution failures
- Consider using a mutating webhook or operator for more robust reconciliation
- Implement metric export (Prometheus) for monitoring resolution success rates
- Add retry logic with exponential backoff for transient network failures

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests RBAC scoping, CronJob scheduling, and in-cluster data backup to a ConfigMap without leaking secrets.

## Key Concepts
- RBAC granularity scoped to a namespace
- CronJob scheduling and Job templates
- Reading Kubernetes events via API in-cluster
- Updating/creating a ConfigMap from a Job

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: events-backup-sa
  namespace: metrics
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: events-backup-role
  namespace: metrics
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["events"]
  verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get","update","create","patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: events-backup-binding
  namespace: metrics
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: events-backup-role
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: events-backup-sa
  namespace: metrics
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: events-backup
  namespace: metrics
spec:
  schedule: "*/2 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: events-backup-sa
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh","-c","kubectl get events -n metrics -o json | jq '.items[0:50]' > /backup/events.json; kubectl create configmap events-backup --from-file=events.json=/backup/events.json -n metrics --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
          - name: backup
            emptyDir: {}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor the ConfigMap growth and avoid hitting 1MiConfigMap limit?
- How would you rollback if the CronJob misbehaves or RBAC scope expands unintentionally?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests comprehensive CKAD skills including per-namespace isolation, configuration management with ConfigMaps and Secrets, InitContainers for dependency setup, sidecar patterns for auxiliary services, health probes for reliability, RBAC for security, and NetworkPolicy for traffic control.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainers for runtime dependency installation
- ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration and credential management
- Sidecar containers for TLS certificate rotation
- Readiness and liveness probes for health monitoring
- Namespace isolation and NetworkPolicy for security boundaries
- Dead-letter queue implementation on PVC storage
- At-least-once delivery semantics with batch processing

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ns-collector
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: install-deps
    image: alpine:latest
    command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache nats-cli']
  containers:
  - name: collector
    image: collector:latest
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: ns-collector-config
    - secretRef:
        name: ns-collector-creds
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health
        port: 8080
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health
        port: 8080
    volumeMounts:
    - name: dlq-pvc
      mountPath: /dlq
  - name: tls-sidecar
    image: tls-sidecar:latest
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tls-certs
      mountPath: /etc/tls
  volumes:
  - name: dlq-pvc
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: dlq-pvc
  - name: tls-certs
    secret:
      secretName: tls-certs
```

## Trade-offs
- **At-least-once vs exactly-once**: At-least-once provides simpler implementation but may cause duplicate processing
- **Sidecar overhead**: TLS rotation adds resource consumption but improves security
- **PVC vs temporary storage**: PVC provides persistence but increases complexity and cost
- **NetworkPolicy restrictions**: Improve security but may impact debugging and monitoring capabilities

```javascript
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: heartbeat-cron
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: install-deps
            image: alpine:3.19
            command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl"]

          - name: heartbeater
            image: alpine:3.19

                name: cron-config
            - secretRef:
                name: target-creds

              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:

                port: 80
```

```yaml
        command: ["sh","-c","cp -r /tls/current/* /certs/ && echo ready > /shared/gateway.pid"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /tls
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /certs
        - name: shared
          mountPath: /shared
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: gateway:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8443
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /tls
        - name: shared
          mountPath: /shared
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8443
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8443
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
      - name: tls-reloader
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh","-c","while true; do inotifywait -e modify,create,attrib /tls/current || true; if [ -f /shared/gateway.pid ]; then kill -USR1 $(cat /shared/gateway.pid); fi; done"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /tls
        - name: shared
          mountPath: /shared
      volumes:
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: gateway-tls
      - name: certs
      - name: shared
        emptyDir: {}
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a one-off reconciliation Job that interacts with external services, ensures idempotent processing via a fingerprint, and properly configures InitContainers, Secrets, and backoff behavior. It also checks handling of PVC-mounted data and rollback planning.


## Key Concepts

- Kubernetes Job with backoff and deadline
- InitContainer for bootstrap tooling
- PVC mounting and data access in a one-off task
- yq for YAML extraction
- Idempotent design via server fingerprint key
- Secret and ConfigMap usage for credentials and endpoints
- Rollback and observability considerations


## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: data-ingest-audit-reconcile
spec:
  backoffLimit: 4
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 900
  template:
    metadata:
      name: data-ingest-audit-reconcile
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reconciler
        image: your-registry/audit-client:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "set -e; /bin/reconcile.sh /data/manifests.yaml"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /data
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq && curl -L -o /usr/local/bin/yq https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/download/v4.9.6/yq_linux_amd64 && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/yq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /data
      restartPolicy: Never
      volumes:
      - name: manifests
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: data-manifests
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: regcred
```

- How would you test idempotency in CI/CD?
- How would you scale this for larger manifest sets without timeouts?
- How would you monitor and rollback on failure?
